topics.name: Wind
topics.kicker: Air moving from high to low pressure · Measured with anemometers
topics.briefing: Wind is air on the move, flowing from areas of high pressure toward areas of low pressure, usually because the Sun heats some places more than others. Earth’s spin bends winds sideways through the Coriolis effect, setting up belts like the steady trade winds, while fast jet streams race high overhead. Sailors judged its strength using a 13-step scale created by Francis Beaufort in 1805.
topics.answerHtml: Wind (accept winds, moving air, or air currents; prompt on air, breeze, or gust; do not accept “air pressure,” “jet stream,” “Coriolis effect,” or a single named wind such as the “trade winds”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Leon Battista Alberti described the first known device for measuring this phenomenon around 1450, and in 1846 Thomas Romney Robinson invented a version that uses spinning cups. Those instruments, called anemometers from a Greek word for this phenomenon, measure its speed.
tossups.r: Vanes point into it to show which way it blows. For 10 points, name this movement of air from high to low pressure.

tossups.p: Robert FitzRoy made one of the first official uses of a 13-level scale for this phenomenon while commanding HMS _Beagle_, and the Royal Navy required it in ship logs from 1838. That scale, created in 1805, originally described its strength by how much sail a warship could carry.
tossups.r: That scale is named for Francis Beaufort and runs from calm at 0 to hurricane force at 12. For 10 points, name this movement of air.

tossups.p: In 1943, a warm, dry chinook [“shih-NOOK”] raised the temperature in Spearfish, South Dakota, by 49 degrees Fahrenheit in just two minutes. Nicknamed “snow eaters,” chinooks are examples of this phenomenon that warm up as they sweep down the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains.
tossups.r: The Santa Ana and the mistral are other local examples. For 10 points, name this movement of air from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure.

tossups.p: Douglas Mawson’s expedition at Antarctica’s Commonwealth Bay faced such fierce examples of this phenomenon that he titled his book about the trip _The Home of the Blizzard_. Those katabatic [“kat-uh-BAT-ik”] flows form when cold, dense air rushes downhill off the ice sheet.
tossups.r: Its speed is measured with an anemometer. For 10 points, name this movement of air, which flows from high to low pressure.

tossups.p: In 1934, observers on New Hampshire’s Mount Washington measured a gust of this phenomenon at 231 miles per hour, a world record, not counting tornadoes, that stood for more than 60 years. A 1996 gust on Australia’s Barrow Island during Cyclone Olivia later beat that record.
tossups.r: Its strength is often ranked on the Beaufort scale. For 10 points, name this movement of air caused by differences in air pressure.

tossups.p: Buys Ballot’s law says that if you stand with your back to this phenomenon in the Northern Hemisphere, low pressure will be on your left. High above the ground, geostrophic examples of it blow parallel to the isobars on a weather map.
tossups.r: Closely spaced isobars mean that it is strong. For 10 points, name this movement of air, which the Coriolis effect bends to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: In the 1920s, Japanese scientist Wasaburo Oishi used weather balloons to find a fast, high-altitude river of this phenomenon, publishing his results in Esperanto. Airliners flying east save time and fuel by riding those jet streams near the top of the troposphere.
tossups.r: The steady trades are examples of it that blow toward the equator. For 10 points, name this movement of air from high to low pressure.

tossups.p: Sailors call the latitudes between 40 and 50 degrees south the “Roaring Forties” because this phenomenon blows so strongly there, with almost no land to slow it down. Farther south lie the “Furious Fifties” and “Screaming Sixties.” Those strong westerlies are one of Earth’s global belts of it.
tossups.r: Its speed is measured by anemometers. For 10 points, name this movement of air, which flows from high pressure to low pressure.

tossups.p: In Homer’s _Odyssey_, Aeolus [“EE-oh-lus”] gives Odysseus a bag holding this phenomenon, but his crew opens it, and the escaping blasts drive the ship back out to sea. In Greek myth, Boreas, Zephyrus, Notus, and Eurus personified it from the north, west, south, and east.
tossups.r: Sand and dust moved by this phenomenon are called aeolian deposits. For 10 points, name this movement of air.

tossups.p: Voyager 2 measured examples of this phenomenon on Neptune moving faster than 2,000 kilometers per hour, the fastest in the solar system. A six-sided jet stream of this phenomenon circles Saturn’s north pole, and on Mars it can lift dust into storms that cover the whole planet.
tossups.r: On Earth, the Coriolis effect bends it to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. For 10 points, name this movement of air from high to low pressure.

tossups.p: In an Aesop fable, the Sun beats the north example of this phenomenon in a contest to make a traveler take off his cloak, because blowing only makes the traveler hold on tighter. Its chilling effect on bare skin makes the air feel colder than the thermometer reads.
tossups.r: Weather vanes point to show where it is coming from. For 10 points, name this movement of air.

tossups.p: On sunny afternoons, land heats up faster than the ocean, so cooler air flows in from the water in a form of this phenomenon; at night the flow reverses. A seasonal version of the same effect brings the summer monsoon to South Asia.
tossups.r: Those daily flows are called sea and land breezes. For 10 points, name this movement of air from high to low pressure.

tossups.p: In 1735, George Hadley explained the steady trades with a giant loop of rising and sinking air, and a second loop of air at middle latitudes was later named for William Ferrel. Sailing ships could be stuck for days in the doldrums near the equator, where this phenomenon is often weak or absent.
tossups.r: Its strength is ranked from calm to hurricane force on the Beaufort scale. For 10 points, name this movement of air.

tossups.p: Over more than two million years, this phenomenon piled up thick layers of fine, yellowish silt called loess [“LUSS”] across China’s Loess Plateau. It also carves rocks into long, streamlined ridges called yardangs, and it makes sand grains hop along the ground in a motion called saltation.
tossups.r: It is caused by differences in air pressure. For 10 points, name this movement of air, which also builds sand dunes.

tossups.p: In 1919, Albert Betz showed that no turbine can capture more than about 59 percent of the kinetic energy carried by this phenomenon. Modern turbines turn that energy into electricity, and offshore farms of them are built at sea, where it blows more steadily.
tossups.r: Its direction is named for where it comes from, so a westerly one blows from the west. For 10 points, name this movement of air from high to low pressure.

clues.t: Air flowing from areas of high pressure toward areas of low pressure
Usually set in motion because the Sun heats Earth’s surface unevenly
Its speed is measured with an anemometer, and a vane shows which way it blows
Named for the direction it comes from: a westerly one blows from the west
Its strength is ranked on the Beaufort scale, from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force)
The Coriolis effect bends it to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
Global belts include the trade ones (blowing toward the equator), the westerlies, and the polar easterlies
Jet streams are fast rivers of it near the top of the troposphere; eastbound airliners ride them to save fuel
Sea breezes blow in from the water on sunny afternoons because land heats faster; land breezes blow out at night
Monsoons are seasonal reversals of it that bring South Asia its summer rains
Local kinds include the warm chinook (“snow eater”) east of the Rockies, California’s Santa Ana, and France’s mistral
George Hadley (1735) explained the trades with a loop of rising and sinking air; a middle-latitude loop is named for William Ferrel; ships stalled in the calm doldrums
Buys Ballot’s law: with your back to it in the Northern Hemisphere, low pressure is on your left; closely spaced isobars mean it is strong
It carries silt that piles up as loess, shapes sand dunes and yardangs, and bounces sand grains along in saltation
It makes bare skin lose heat faster, so the air feels colder than the thermometer reads
Leon Battista Alberti described the first known device to measure it (around 1450); Thomas Romney Robinson invented the cup anemometer (1846)
Francis Beaufort created his scale in 1805, based on how much sail a warship could carry; Robert FitzRoy used it on HMS _Beagle_
In 1943, a chinook raised the temperature in Spearfish, South Dakota, by 49 °F in two minutes
Douglas Mawson’s base at Antarctica’s Commonwealth Bay had such fierce katabatic flows that he called his book _The Home of the Blizzard_
Observers on New Hampshire’s Mount Washington measured a 231-mile-per-hour gust in 1934, the record (not counting tornadoes) until a 1996 gust on Australia’s Barrow Island
Wasaburo Oishi found the jet stream over Japan with weather balloons in the 1920s and published his results in Esperanto
The “Roaring Forties” (40 to 50 degrees south) have strong westerlies with little land to slow them, followed by the “Furious Fifties”
In the _Odyssey_, Aeolus gives Odysseus a bag holding it; Boreas, Zephyrus, Notus, and Eurus personified it in Greek myth
Neptune’s are the fastest in the solar system, over 2,000 km per hour; Saturn has a six-sided jet stream; Mars has planet-wide dust storms
In an Aesop fable, the Sun beats the north one in a contest to make a traveler take off his cloak
Albert Betz showed in 1919 that a turbine can capture at most about 59 percent of its kinetic energy

trap.title: Moving air, not pressure
trap.body: Wind tossups mention high and low pressure, isobars, the Coriolis effect, and jet streams, so players blurt out “air pressure,” “Coriolis effect,” or “jet stream.” Those are separate answers: pressure differences cause wind, the Coriolis effect bends it, and a jet stream is one fast band of it. Naming one particular wind, like the trade winds, is wrong when the question wants wind in general.
trap.fix: If the giveaway asks for the movement of air itself, measured by anemometers and ranked on the Beaufort scale, say wind. Remember that a wind is named for the direction it comes from, so a north wind blows toward the south.
trap.line: Real answer line: Wind (accept moving air; prompt on air; do not accept “air pressure” or “Coriolis effect”)

topics.name: Mohs hardness scale
topics.kicker: Ranks minerals 1 to 10 by scratch resistance · Talc is 1, diamond is 10
topics.briefing: The Mohs hardness scale ranks minerals by how well they resist scratching, from soft talc at 1 to diamond at 10. German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs created it in 1812 around a simple rule: a harder mineral scratches a softer one. Geologists test unknown minerals with a fingernail (about 2.5), a copper penny (about 3 to 3.5), or a steel knife (about 5.5), and the steps are uneven: diamond resists scratching nearly four times as well as corundum, ranked 9.
topics.answerHtml: Mohs hardness scale (accept Mohs scale or hardness; prompt on scratch test; do not accept “Richter scale,” “Moho,” or other hardness tests such as “Rockwell” or “Vickers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Statisticians often use this scale as a textbook example of an ordinal scale, because its numbers show only rank order and not equal steps. In actual scratch resistance, the gap between its 9 and 10 is bigger than all of the other gaps put together.
tossups.r: It runs from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. For 10 points, name this scale that ranks minerals by how well they resist scratching.

tossups.p: Scientists measuring scratch resistance with a sclerometer [“skleh-ROM-uh-ter”] found that corundum, ranked 9 on this scale, resists scratching about twice as well as topaz, ranked 8. The mineral ranked 10 does nearly four times as well as corundum.
tossups.r: That top mineral is diamond, and talc sits at the bottom. For 10 points, name this scale of mineral scratch resistance created by a German mineralogist in 1812.

tossups.p: A German mineralogist created this scale in 1812, choosing ten readily available minerals as its reference points. It works on a simple rule: a mineral can scratch any mineral ranked below it, but not one ranked above it.
tossups.r: Quartz ranks 7 on this scale. For 10 points, name this scale that runs from talc at 1 to diamond at 10.

tossups.p: Geologists in the field estimate where a mineral falls on this scale with simple tools: a fingernail rates about 2.5, a copper penny about 3 to 3.5, a steel knife or a piece of glass about 5.5, and a steel file about 6.5.
tossups.r: Talc, the softest mineral, sits at the bottom of this scale. For 10 points, name this scale that ranks minerals from 1 to 10 by how well they resist scratching.

tossups.p: Jade is tough enough to resist breaking but ranks only about 6 to 7 on this scale, while some minerals that rank far higher can shatter if struck the right way. That difference shows that this scale measures resistance to scratching, not toughness.
tossups.r: Quartz ranks 7 and corundum ranks 9 on this scale. For 10 points, name this scale topped by diamond at 10.

tossups.p: Unlike the Brinell and Vickers tests, which press a steel ball or a diamond point into metals and measure the dent, this scale simply asks which mineral scratches which. Its ten reference minerals were chosen in 1812 because they were easy to find.
tossups.r: Its softest mineral is talc and its top mineral is diamond. For 10 points, name this 1-to-10 scale used to identify minerals.

tossups.p: Tooth enamel, made mostly of a form of apatite, ranks about 5 on this scale, the same spot as apatite itself. The mineral just below apatite on this scale, fluorite, gave its name to fluorescence because some samples glow under ultraviolet light.
tossups.r: Gypsum, which a fingernail can scratch, ranks 2 on this scale. For 10 points, name this scale that runs from talc to diamond.

tossups.p: Orthoclase, a feldspar whose name means “straight break” in Greek, marks 6 on this scale, which makes it just able to scratch window glass. Plagioclase, the other main kind of feldspar, ranks about the same, at 6 to 6.5.
tossups.r: Quartz, one step above orthoclase, ranks 7. For 10 points, name this scale that ranks minerals by how well they resist scratching, topped by diamond.

tossups.p: Jewelers warn that gems ranking below 7 on this scale can slowly be scratched by ordinary household dust, which contains tiny grains of a common mineral ranked 7. Topaz, the November birthstone, ranks 8, and emery, a dark rock rich in the mineral ranked 9, coats nail files and sandpaper.
tossups.r: That mineral, corundum, includes rubies and sapphires. For 10 points, name this scale of mineral scratch resistance topped by diamond.

tossups.p: Soapstone, a soft carving stone, is made mostly of the mineral at the bottom of this scale, which feels greasy and is ground into a soft powder used in cosmetics. Gypsum, the next mineral up, is heated to make plaster of Paris and used in drywall.
tossups.r: That bottom mineral, talc, ranks 1, and diamond ranks 10. For 10 points, name this scale of mineral scratch resistance.

tossups.p: Clear crystals of the mineral ranked 3 on this scale, called Iceland spar, make objects seen through them look doubled, and that mineral fizzes in weak acid. It can be scratched by a steel knife but not by a fingernail.
tossups.r: That mineral, calcite, sits between gypsum and fluorite on this scale. For 10 points, name this scale that runs from talc at 1 to diamond at 10.

tossups.p: Students memorize the order of this scale’s ten minerals with sentences like “Tall Giraffes Can Find Alligators Or Quaint Tigers Chewing Dinner.” In that sentence, the words “Find” and “Alligators” stand for fluorite and apatite, ranked 4 and 5.
tossups.r: The first word stands for talc and the last for diamond. For 10 points, name this scale of mineral scratch resistance from 1 to 10.

tossups.p: An unglazed porcelain streak plate ranks about 6.5 to 7 on this scale, so minerals that rank higher scratch the plate instead of leaving a colored streak. Along with streak, luster, and cleavage, a mineral’s place on this scale helps geologists identify it.
tossups.r: It ranks talc at 1 and diamond at 10. For 10 points, name this scale used to compare how easily minerals are scratched.

tossups.p: Volcanic glass called obsidian rates about 5 to 5.5 on this scale, while olivine, known as the green gem peridot, rates about 6.5 to 7. Because ordinary glass rates about 5.5, minerals above that point can scratch a window.
tossups.r: Diamond, a form of pure carbon, sits at the top of this scale at 10. For 10 points, name this scale that ranks minerals by scratch resistance.

tossups.p: The creator of this scale studied under Abraham Werner, the leader of the Neptunists, at Germany’s Freiberg Mining Academy. He picked ten minerals that were easy to get as its fixed points, but later measurements showed that the steps between them are very uneven.
tossups.r: It is sometimes confused with the Richter scale for earthquakes. For 10 points, name this scale that runs from talc at 1 to diamond at 10.

clues.t: Ranks minerals from 1 to 10 by how well they resist scratching
Talc, the softest, is 1, and diamond is 10, at the top
Quartz ranks 7, so it scratches glass
Its rule: a mineral can scratch any mineral ranked below it, but not one ranked above it
Created in 1812 by a German mineralogist, first name Friedrich, who gave it his last name
Its ten minerals, in order: talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz, topaz, corundum, diamond
Field tests: a fingernail is about 2.5, a copper penny about 3 to 3.5, a steel knife or glass about 5.5, a steel file about 6.5
Relative, not evenly spaced: diamond resists scratching nearly four times as well as corundum
Corundum ranks 9; rubies and sapphires are forms of corundum
Orthoclase, a feldspar whose name means “straight break,” ranks 6 and can just scratch window glass
Gypsum ranks 2, so a fingernail can scratch it; it is used in plaster of Paris and drywall
Calcite ranks 3; it fizzes in weak acid, and its clear Iceland spar crystals make objects look doubled
Apatite ranks 5, about the same as tooth enamel; fluorite, at 4, gave fluorescence its name
It measures scratch resistance, not toughness: tough jade ranks only about 6 to 7
A mnemonic for its order: “Tall Giraffes Can Find Alligators Or Quaint Tigers Chewing Dinner”
Statisticians use it as a classic ordinal scale; the gap between 9 and 10 is bigger than all the other gaps combined
Sclerometer measurements show corundum resists scratching about twice as well as topaz, and diamond nearly four times as well as corundum
Unlike the Brinell and Vickers tests, which press a ball or diamond point into metal, it compares which mineral scratches which
An unglazed porcelain streak plate rates about 6.5 to 7; higher-ranked minerals scratch it instead of leaving a streak
Household dust contains quartz grains, so gems ranked below 7 can slowly get scratched
Topaz, the November birthstone, ranks 8; emery, a rock rich in corundum, coats nail files and sandpaper
Soapstone, a soft carving stone, is mostly talc, which feels greasy and is ground into powder
Obsidian rates about 5 to 5.5 and olivine (the gem peridot) about 6.5 to 7; window glass is about 5.5
Its creator studied under Abraham Werner, leader of the Neptunists, at Germany’s Freiberg Mining Academy

trap.title: Not Richter, not the Moho
trap.body: This scale ranks minerals by how well they resist scratching, so it has nothing to do with earthquakes; the Richter scale measures earthquake size. The Moho, short for the Mohorovičić discontinuity, is the boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle. Some real tossups ask for the property, hardness, instead of the scale named for Friedrich Mohs, and both are accepted here.
trap.fix: Talc to diamond, quartz at 7, fingernails and steel knives, and scratch tests mean the Mohs scale (or hardness). Earthquakes mean the Richter or moment magnitude scale, and a boundary deep beneath the crust means the Moho.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mohs hardness scale (accept hardness or Mohs scale; do not accept “Richter scale”)
